builder_plan.scenario: Your coding assistant makes changes that still need substantial repair before merging.
builder_plan.change: Try the technique on held-out issues from a repository with reliable tests.
builder_plan.baseline: The same coding agent, repository snapshot, tools, and token budget.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Correct patches, regression failures, human repair time, and total cost per accepted change.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Reducing Inference Cost of Coding Agents with Timeout Cascades
summary: The method replaces always routing coding-agent tasks to a large model with a timeout cascade: a small cheap model attempts the task first and escalates to a large model only on failure or timeout, eliminating the need for a learned task router. It costs the added latency of wasted small-model attempts on hard tasks plus modest orchestration logic, while accuracy is reported as preserved. It can fail if the workload skews toward hard tasks (the small model then adds cost without benefit), if the timeout threshold is miscalibrated, or if the small model produces plausible-but-wrong outputs that are not detected as failures and therefore never escalate.
rationale: The cascade requires no trained router or extra infrastructure, works with small open-weight models that fit a 24 GB GPU, and the cost reduction is demonstrated on a standard benchmark without accuracy loss.
technique: Small-to-large model timeout cascade for coding agents

It costs the added latency of wasted small-model attempts on hard tasks plus modest orchestration logic, while accuracy is reported as preserved. It can fail if the workload skews toward hard tasks (the small model then adds cost without benefit), if the timeout threshold is miscalibrated, or if the small model produces plausible-but-wrong outputs that are not detected as failures and therefore never escalate.
